q: Why is it significant that cells oxidise glucose in many small, enzyme-catalysed steps rather than in one step, as in burning?
options: Stepwise oxidation releases more total energy per glucose than combustion, raising the ATP yield
Energy is released in small amounts that can be captured in ATP rather than mostly lost as heat
Enzymes supply the activation energy for each step, so the cell never has to invest any ATP
Each extra step creates a small amount of new energy, so longer pathways give higher yields
explanation: The total energy released by oxidising glucose (~2870 kJ/mol) is the same whether it is burned or respired – the pathway can't change it, and energy is never created. Releasing it in small, enzyme-controlled steps lets portions be coupled to ATP synthesis (~30–32 ATP per glucose) instead of being lost all at once as heat. Enzymes lower activation energy; they don't supply energy (glycolysis even invests 2 ATP).
